COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- Sri Lanka President Mahinda Rajapaksa claimed Friday there was "a conspiracy with certain international forces" to belittle his government's military victories against Tamil Tiger rebels. Sri Lankan army troops have had there most decisive victories against the Tamil Tigers in recent weeks. The aim of these conspirators, he said in an address to the nation, "is to level unfounded charges against the army commander who works with greatest dedication to achieve these victories." He also used the address to formally announce the recapture of the northern town of Elephant Pass, the point at which mainland Sri Lanka links to the northern Jaffna peninsula. It had remained in rebel hands for over nine years. The recapture enable the government to use the A-9 highway linking the mainland to the peninsula to move troops and supplies. Until now it was done either by air or by sea. Rajapaksa's remarks came amid mounting attacks on the media. On Tuesday a group armed with rifles, pistols and grenades attacked the country's most popular privately owned television channel MTV. The main control room equipment costing more than $ 1.7 million was damaged. On Thursday, Lasantha Wickrematunga, chief editor of The Sunday Leader, a newspaper which had exposed corruption and criticized aspects of ongoing military operations, was shot dead. Earlier Friday, the leader of the main opposition United National Party (UNP), Ranil Wickremasinghe, accused military and security officials of the attacks, saying the government could not control them. "Armed forces members are shocked about these incidents. The armed forces says due to the activities of few intelligence sections, the reputation of the country is being ruined. That is the team which the government has no control of," he told parliament. Rajapaksa said there were efforts to belittle military victories "to turn the attention of the people to other directions." He said such "conspiracies arise when a country moves ahead without giving in to external pressures." He added "one must not mistake these conspiracies as being against me or my government. This is a conspiracy against the entire country by those who have been driven to fear due to the successes of our security forces." Meanwhile, fighting in northern Sri Lanka between government and rebel forces escalated on several fronts Friday, while Tamil Tiger rebels killed seven people in a roadside bombing. Three members of the Sri Lankan air force and four civilians died when rebels exploded a claymore landmine in the village of Morawewa, near the northeastern port city of Trincomalee, police said. The strategic port town is located about 240km (150 miles) north of the capital, Colombo. Friday's incident came as troops pursued their military campaign in the northern Wanni region to recapture remaining rebel strongholds, military sources said. Government troops were said to be meeting fierce resistance as they advanced on the Tamil stronghold of Mullaitivu and a naval blockade remained in the northeastern seas. The 25-year long civil war has left more than 65,000 people dead. The U.S. State Department has designated the Tamil Tigers a terrorist organization.

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) —** Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa said Friday that “certain international forces” were involved in a plot to diminish the significance of his government’s battlefield successes against the Tamil Tiger rebels.

In recent weeks, Sri Lankan soldiers have achieved their most decisive victories yet against the Tigers. In a national address, Rajapaksa said the alleged conspirators intended to make baseless accusations against the army commander, whom he described as working with exceptional commitment to secure those gains.

During the speech, the president also officially confirmed that government forces had retaken Elephant Pass, a northern town connecting mainland Sri Lanka with the Jaffna Peninsula. The area had been controlled by the rebels for more than nine years.

Regaining Elephant Pass allows the government to transport soldiers and supplies along the A-9 highway between the mainland and the peninsula. Previously, such movements had to be carried out by air or sea.

Rajapaksa made his comments as violence against Sri Lanka’s media was increasing. On Tuesday, assailants carrying rifles, handguns and grenades attacked MTV, the country’s most-watched privately owned television station. Equipment in its main control room valued at more than $1.7 million was damaged.

Two days later, Lasantha Wickrematunga, editor in chief of *The Sunday Leader*, was shot and killed. His newspaper had reported on corruption and criticized elements of the continuing military campaign.

Earlier Friday, Ranil Wickremasinghe, head of the principal opposition United National Party, alleged that military and security personnel were responsible for the attacks and said the government was unable to restrain them.

Speaking in parliament, Wickremasinghe said members of the armed forces were disturbed by the incidents. He added that, according to the military, the conduct of a small number of intelligence units was harming Sri Lanka’s reputation and that this group was beyond government control.

Rajapaksa argued that attempts were being made to downplay the military’s achievements and divert public attention elsewhere. He said such plots emerge when a nation advances without yielding to pressure from abroad.

He further warned that the alleged conspiracy should not be viewed as directed solely at him or his administration. Instead, he characterized it as an attack on the whole country by people frightened by the security forces’ successes.

At the same time, combat between government troops and rebel forces intensified Friday across several fronts in northern Sri Lanka. Tamil Tiger insurgents also killed seven people with a roadside bomb.

Police said three Sri Lankan air force personnel and four civilians died when rebels detonated a claymore mine in Morawewa, a village near the northeastern port city of Trincomalee. The strategically important port lies approximately 240 kilometers, or 150 miles, north of Colombo.

The bombing occurred while government troops continued their offensive in the northern Wanni region, seeking to capture the rebels’ remaining bases, according to military sources.

Government forces reportedly encountered strong resistance as they moved toward the Tamil stronghold of Mullaitivu. A naval blockade also remained in place in waters off the northeast.

More than 65,000 people have been killed during the 25-year civil war. The U.S. State Department classifies the Tamil Tigers as a terrorist organization.

His comments came as opposition politicians and media organizations raised alarm over a series of violent attacks on journalists and independent news outlets, alleging that elements connected to the security establishment were responsible.

Government forces had recently recaptured Elephant Pass, a strategically important causeway linking the Jaffna Peninsula with the rest of the island. The victory gave the army control of the northern stretch of the A-9 highway, allowing troops, equipment and supplies to be transported by land to Jaffna. For years, access to the peninsula had been constrained by fighting and rebel control of key territory, forcing the government to rely heavily on sea and air routes.

Rajapaksa portrayed the advance as a decisive step in the campaign to defeat the Tamil Tigers and restore government authority across the north. He argued, however, that hostile groups inside and outside Sri Lanka were trying to weaken the impact of the victory by creating instability and damaging the country’s international reputation. The president did not provide detailed evidence of a coordinated foreign conspiracy, but his remarks reflected the administration’s longstanding claim that critics of the war were assisting the rebels, deliberately or otherwise.

The military success was accompanied by growing concern about press freedom. Critical media institutions and prominent journalists had faced intimidation, threats and violent attacks. Opposition leaders argued that the timing and apparent coordination of some incidents pointed to the involvement—or at least the knowledge—of people within the security apparatus. Government officials denied responsibility and said the allegations were politically motivated.

Media groups countered that the authorities had repeatedly failed to identify or prosecute those behind attacks on journalists. They warned that a climate of impunity was encouraging further violence and forcing reporters to censor themselves, particularly when covering military operations, alleged corruption or abuses by state officials.

The recapture of Elephant Pass therefore represented both a major strategic gain and a difficult political test for the Rajapaksa government. While the reopening of the A-9 highway strengthened the army’s position and improved its ability to support forces in Jaffna, escalating violence against the media raised serious questions about democratic accountability. The government’s battlefield advances were widely celebrated by its supporters, but critics maintained that military victory could not justify attacks on dissent or the erosion of press freedom.

counterfactuals.output:
**Rajapaksa alleges foreign plot after key victory over Tamil Tigers**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has accused unnamed international forces of conspiring to undermine the military’s victories over the Tamil Tiger rebels, as government troops announced the recapture of the strategic Elephant Pass causeway.

In a televised address, Rajapaksa said outside groups were attempting to tarnish the army’s campaign against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE. He did not provide evidence or identify those he said were involved.

The president’s comments came after the military said troops had taken control of Elephant Pass, the narrow land corridor connecting the Jaffna Peninsula with the rest of northern Sri Lanka. The area had been held by the rebels since 2000 and was viewed as a strategically and symbolically important objective.

The advance followed the fall of Kilinochchi, the LTTE’s former administrative center, and left the rebels confined to a shrinking area in the northeast. The Tigers have fought since 1983 for an independent homeland for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority.

Independent confirmation of battlefield developments remained difficult because journalists and aid workers faced tight restrictions in the conflict zone. Both sides have previously been accused of human rights violations, allegations they have denied.

Rajapaksa’s remarks also came amid growing concern over attacks on Sri Lankan journalists.

Prominent newspaper editor Lasantha Wickrematunge, a fierce government critic, was shot by unidentified gunmen near Colombo and later died of his injuries. Days earlier, armed men stormed and damaged a private television station known for reporting critical of the government.

Sri Lankan officials condemned the attacks and promised investigations. Media organizations and opposition politicians, however, said the violence had intensified a climate of fear and called on authorities to ensure the cases were independently investigated.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for either attack.

**Sri Lankan troops seize Elephant Pass as president hails advance; attacks on media deepen fears**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka, Jan. 9, 2009** — Sri Lankan government forces captured the strategic Elephant Pass gateway to the Jaffna Peninsula on Friday, President Mahinda Rajapaksa announced, marking another major battlefield setback for the separatist Tamil Tigers as violence and intimidation against the country’s media intensified.

In a nationally televised address, Rajapaksa said troops had taken full control of Elephant Pass, a narrow strip of land connecting the northern mainland with Jaffna. He portrayed the victory as a decisive step in the government’s campaign to defeat the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, after more than a quarter-century of civil war.

The announcement came a week after the military seized Kilinochchi, the rebels’ former administrative capital. Together, the two advances have dismantled key parts of the LTTE’s conventional defenses and restored government control over much of the A9 highway, the principal land route linking Jaffna with the rest of Sri Lanka.

“Our heroic forces have liberated Elephant Pass,” Rajapaksa said, congratulating soldiers and calling on the rebels to lay down their arms. He said the campaign was directed against terrorism rather than the ethnic Tamil population and promised that civilians in the north would be protected.

The military said troops advancing from the south and from government-held positions on the Jaffna Peninsula forced rebel units to withdraw from the area. Elephant Pass had long been regarded as one of the most important military positions in northern Sri Lanka. The LTTE captured the base from government forces in 2000 after a prolonged offensive, in one of the most humiliating defeats suffered by the army during the war.

Its recapture carries both strategic and symbolic weight. Control of the pass eases the army’s ability to move personnel and supplies overland to Jaffna, which for years depended heavily on sea and air transport. It also leaves the Tigers confined largely to a shrinking area in the northeast, particularly parts of Mullaitivu district.

Independent confirmation of battlefield claims was not immediately possible. The government has severely restricted journalists’ access to the front, while the LTTE also tightly controls information from territory under its authority. Neither side’s casualty figures can be reliably verified.

### Civilians trapped by shrinking front

The military’s rapid advance has raised mounting concern for civilians caught between the opposing forces. Tens of thousands of people have been displaced repeatedly as fighting has moved eastward, according to humanitarian agencies. Aid groups have warned of shortages of food, medicine and shelter in areas still held by the rebels.

The government accuses the LTTE of preventing civilians from leaving and using them as human shields, a charge the rebels deny. Tamil groups and relief workers, meanwhile, have alleged that government shelling has endangered populated areas. Colombo says its forces are under orders to minimize civilian casualties.

The United Nations and international humanitarian organizations have urged both sides to allow civilians to move to safety and to ensure access for relief supplies.

The LTTE, which has fought since 1983 for an independent Tamil state in the north and east, once controlled extensive territory and operated a conventional army, naval wing and rudimentary air force. The organization says it is defending Tamils from decades of discrimination by the Sinhalese-majority state. It is banned as a terrorist organization by Sri Lanka, the United States, India, the European Union and several other governments.

More than 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict erupted, though the true toll is uncertain.

### Editor’s killing shocks Colombo

The government’s battlefield announcement was overshadowed in the capital by outrage over the assassination Thursday of Lasantha Wickrematunge, one of Sri Lanka’s best-known newspaper editors and a fierce critic of the Rajapaksa administration.

Wickrematunge, editor of *The Sunday Leader*, was shot by motorcycle-riding assailants as he drove to work near Colombo. He died after being taken to a hospital. No group immediately claimed responsibility.

Colleagues said Wickrematunge had received repeated death threats because of his reporting on corruption, alleged government abuses and the conduct of the war. His newspaper had also faced lawsuits, threats and attacks.

Rajapaksa condemned the killing and ordered an investigation, describing Wickrematunge as a friend despite their political differences. Opposition politicians, press-freedom organizations and journalists said the assassination reflected a climate in which government critics could be threatened or attacked with impunity.

The killing followed a pre-dawn assault Tuesday on the studios of the Maharaja Television network, which operates Sirasa TV and other outlets. Armed men stormed the compound, damaged equipment and set part of the facility ablaze. The network had been accused by nationalist groups of giving excessive coverage to opposition voices and of reporting the war in a manner unfavorable to the government.

No arrests were immediately announced in either attack.

Journalists in Sri Lanka have faced killings, abductions, assaults and intimidation throughout the conflict. Tamil journalists have been particularly vulnerable, but Sinhalese and Muslim reporters critical of the government or security forces have also been targeted. Rights organizations say investigations rarely lead to prosecutions.

Government officials deny directing attacks on the press and say journalists remain free to report, subject to restrictions needed for national security. Media advocates argue that inflammatory statements by officials and pro-government commentators have helped create a dangerous environment for dissent.

As celebrations over Elephant Pass began among government supporters, Wickrematunge’s death underscored a darker dimension of the campaign’s final phase: Sri Lanka’s military is advancing rapidly, but scrutiny of the war—and of those prosecuting it—is becoming increasingly perilous.

With the LTTE pushed into a narrowing pocket of territory, the government appears closer than at any point in decades to destroying the rebels’ conventional military structure. Yet the fate of trapped civilians, the possibility of prolonged guerrilla warfare and the absence of a political settlement addressing Tamil grievances remain unresolved.

For Colombo, Friday brought one of the government’s most significant battlefield victories. For the country’s embattled press, it brought renewed questions about whether criticism can survive alongside the war.

- **Military campaign against the Tamil Tigers (LTTE):** Government forces captured the LTTE’s administrative capital, **Kilinochchi**, and then the strategic **Elephant Pass** corridor. - **Roadside bombing near Trincomalee:** A roadside bomb exploded in the eastern Trincomalee region, causing deaths and injuries among security personnel and/or civilians. Authorities blamed the LTTE, treating the attack as evidence that the rebels could still conduct bombings outside their shrinking northern stronghold.

- **Attacks on the media:** Armed men raided and badly damaged the studios of **MTV/Maharaja Television**, whose outlets included Sirasa TV. Soon afterward, *Sunday Leader* editor **Lasantha Wickrematunga**, a prominent government critic, was shot dead near Colombo.

- **Opposition allegations:** Opposition politicians alleged that elements of the state security apparatus—or groups acting with official protection—were involved in both the MTV attack and Wickrematunga’s assassination. The government denied responsibility and promised investigations, but critics pointed to the attackers’ apparent ability to operate in heavily secured areas and escape without arrest.

**Sri Lankan army retakes strategic Elephant Pass amid press-freedom fears**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka, Jan. 9, 2009** — Sri Lankan troops have recaptured Elephant Pass, the narrow gateway to the northern Jaffna Peninsula, giving the government control of a strategically important section of the A-9 highway as its campaign against the Tamil Tiger rebels gathers momentum.

President Mahinda Rajapaksa announced the victory days after the military seized Kilinochchi, the rebels’ administrative capital. The advances have pushed the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, into a shrinking area of northeastern Sri Lanka after more than two decades of civil war.

Elephant Pass has long been one of the conflict’s most important military positions. The strip of land controls the main ground approach to Jaffna, where hundreds of thousands of civilians live and where the government maintains a large military presence. The LTTE captured the base in 2000, forcing the army to rely heavily on costly sea and air transport to supply forces on the peninsula.

Control of Elephant Pass and the A-9, the main north-south highway, could eventually restore an overland supply route between Jaffna and government-held territory. It would make troop movements and civilian commerce easier, while further dividing rebel positions in the north.

The road, however, cannot immediately return to normal use. Fighting, mines, damaged infrastructure and security checks are likely to delay reopening, and the LTTE retains the ability to carry out ambushes and bombings even after losing conventional territory.

Rajapaksa has presented the military victories as proof that the separatist movement is nearing defeat. He has also accused unnamed foreign and domestic forces of conspiring to undermine the war effort and reverse the government’s gains. Such allegations have frequently been directed at critics accused of weakening national unity or damaging Sri Lanka’s image abroad.

The president has not publicly produced detailed evidence for a coordinated foreign conspiracy. Opposition politicians, rights groups and journalists say the rhetoric risks branding dissenters and independent reporters as traitors.

Those concerns have intensified amid a worsening press-freedom crisis. Lasantha Wickrematunge, editor of *The Sunday Leader* and a prominent government critic, was shot dead near Colombo on Thursday. Earlier in the week, armed attackers destroyed equipment at the studios of the privately owned MTV/Sirasa television network.

Wickrematunge’s killing followed years of assaults, threats, disappearances and legal pressure against Sri Lankan journalists. Media organizations say many reporters have fled the country, while others practice self-censorship because of fears for their safety.

The government has denied involvement in attacks on the media and has promised investigations. Rajapaksa condemned Wickrematunge’s murder. Press-freedom advocates, however, say previous cases have rarely resulted in convictions and are calling for independent inquiries.

The recapture of Elephant Pass therefore marks both a major military and symbolic victory for Rajapaksa’s government. But it comes as the administration faces growing questions over civilian protection, political intolerance and whether the defeat of the LTTE will be accompanied by greater democratic freedom.

**Sri Lankan troops close in on rebel stronghold as fears grow for civilians**  
*January 12, 2009*

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan troops pressed toward the northeastern town of Mullaitivu on Monday after a series of major victories over the Tamil Tiger rebels, while President Mahinda Rajapaksa defended the military campaign amid growing concern about civilian casualties and attacks on independent journalists.

Government forces captured Kilinochchi, the rebels’ administrative capital, on January 2 and took control of the strategically important Elephant Pass causeway a week later. The victories reopened the land route to the Jaffna Peninsula and confined the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, to a shrinking area of jungle and coastline in the northeast.

Military officials said several army divisions were advancing on Mullaitivu, the guerrillas’ last major town and their principal military base. The government has barred most independent journalists and aid workers from the battle zone, making battlefield claims by either side difficult to verify.

Rajapaksa, who has made the defeat of the LTTE the central objective of his presidency, praised the armed forces and said the offensive was intended to free Tamil civilians from rebel control rather than target the Tamil community.

The government says troops have been instructed to minimize civilian casualties. It accuses the Tigers of forcing residents to retreat with them, conscripting children and using populated areas for military purposes. The LTTE and Tamil advocacy groups accuse the army of shelling civilian areas, a charge the military denies.

United Nations agencies estimate that hundreds of thousands of civilians remain inside rebel-held territory in the Vanni region. Many have been displaced repeatedly as the front lines move eastward. Food, medicine, shelter and clean water are increasingly scarce, according to humanitarian organizations, which have called for safe access to people trapped by the fighting.

The offensive has coincided with renewed fears about press freedom following the killing of Lasantha Wickrematunge, editor of the *Sunday Leader* newspaper and one of the government’s most prominent critics.

Wickrematunge was shot by motorcycle-riding assailants on January 8 while driving to work near Colombo. He died after being taken to a hospital. No group claimed responsibility.

His newspaper had regularly investigated corruption and criticized both the government’s conduct of the war and the LTTE’s violence. Wickrematunge had said that he expected to be killed and wrote a posthumously published editorial blaming the government for creating a climate in which dissenters could be attacked.

Rajapaksa condemned the murder and ordered an investigation. His administration rejected allegations that it was responsible, describing the killing as an effort to discredit the government and its military victories. Journalists’ organizations said previous abductions, assaults and killings had rarely resulted in successful prosecutions.

Sri Lanka’s conflict began in 1983 after years of tension between the Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority. Tamil grievances included discriminatory language and education policies, unequal access to state employment and violence by security forces and mobs. Anti-Tamil riots in July 1983, in which hundreds and possibly more than 1,000 people were killed, helped propel the country into full-scale war.

The LTTE, led by Velupillai Prabhakaran, emerged as the dominant Tamil militant organization and fought for an independent state called Tamil Eelam in the north and east. It eliminated rival Tamil groups and became notorious for suicide bombings and political assassinations. Its victims included former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993.

Government forces have also been accused of extrajudicial killings, disappearances, torture and indiscriminate attacks during successive phases of the war.

India sent peacekeeping troops to Sri Lanka in 1987 but withdrew in 1990 after fighting the Tigers. A Norwegian-brokered ceasefire signed in 2002 raised hopes for a negotiated settlement, but talks collapsed and large-scale warfare resumed by 2006. The government formally withdrew from the ceasefire in January 2008.

At least 70,000 people are estimated to have died during the conflict, although no definitive toll exists. Hundreds of thousands more have been displaced, and tens of thousands have fled abroad.

With Kilinochchi and Elephant Pass lost, the Tigers face their most serious military crisis. Yet diplomats and analysts warn that capturing territory may not resolve the underlying ethnic grievances that sustained the rebellion. As troops approach Mullaitivu, the immediate concern is the fate of civilians crowded into the rapidly contracting war zone.
